client: I've been really stressed out lately because my final exams are coming up next week and I just don't feel ready at all. I've been working so many hours at my part-time job that I barely have time to sit down and actually study. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix the fact that I have way too much on my plate right now.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely overwhelming — exams looming, long work hours, and barely a moment to breathe, and I can hear that pressure in the urgency of your voice. You're right that talking won't magically clear your schedule, but it can help us untangle which thoughts might be making this feel even more unmanageable than it already is. I'm wondering — when you say you don't feel ready, is that based on where your preparation actually stands, or is exhaustion making it hard to see what you *have* already done?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I think it's probably both, but I lean toward saying the exhaustion is making everything look worse than it is. Like, I know I've studied some of the material, but when I sit down to review it, my brain just goes blank and I start panicking that none of it stuck. And then that panic eats up more time, and I end up just staring at my notes feeling like I've already failed before the exam even happens.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of tense energy — really matches what you're describing, that spiral where panic takes over before you've even given yourself a chance. What you're identifying is actually a really important pattern: the blank mind isn't proof that nothing stuck, it's a symptom of anxiety hijacking your ability to access what you *do* know. Can we gently challenge that thought — "I've already failed" — by asking what small, concrete evidence exists that you *have* prepared, even imperfectly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess... okay, I did spend three nights going over my notes, and I did practice answering questions out loud a few times. But the thing is, when I'm actually sitting there in the exam room and my mind goes blank, none of that feels real anymore — it's like it never happened. So even if I try to remind myself "you prepared," my brain just doesn't believe it in that moment, and I don't know how to make it believe it.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now really reflects that feeling of your thoughts racing ahead of you, and it makes sense — you're describing one of anxiety's cruelest tricks, where it erases your own evidence in the moment you need it most. What you're experiencing is called "state-dependent memory," where high anxiety can temporarily block access to what you know, but here's the important reframe: your brain going blank in the exam is *not* the same as the information being gone. One practical CBT tool is to write a small "evidence card" beforehand — literally a few lines reminding yourself of those three study nights and the practice questions — so your rational mind has already done the work of believing it *before* the panic hits.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean, the evidence card idea sounds nice in theory, but I honestly don't know if I'd even remember to look at it when I'm sitting there in a panic. Like, when my heart is pounding and everything goes blank, the last thing I'm thinking about is pulling out some card I wrote the night before. And even if I did look at it, part of me worries I'd just read it and think "yeah but that was then, and right now I clearly don't know anything."
therapist: There's something really telling in the way you're speaking right now — your voice has gone quieter, almost like a part of you is bracing for disappointment even as you're talking through this, and that exhaustion comes through clearly. What you're describing is the anxiety essentially arguing against every tool before you've even tried it, which is itself worth noticing — your brain is working very hard to protect the belief that failure is inevitable. So rather than the card being something you *remember* to reach for, what if we made it a ritual you practice *before* the exam, so that the self-reassurance becomes the habit, not just the card?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, the part about my brain working hard to protect the belief that failure is inevitable... that actually landed differently than I expected. Like, I hadn't thought of it that way before, that the anxiety is almost doing its job too well. But when you say "ritual before the exam," I get this immediate sinking feeling, because my mornings before tests are already so chaotic and rushed that I can't imagine carving out any calm space for something like that.
therapist: That realization — that anxiety is almost *too* good at its job — is genuinely meaningful, and I can hear that it opened something up for you even as your voice stays soft and a little guarded, like you're holding both the insight and the worry at the same time. You don't need a perfect, calm morning ritual — even taking three slow breaths in the hallway outside the exam room, or reading one grounding sentence on your phone, counts as anchoring yourself before you walk in. The goal isn't to eliminate the chaos of your morning, it's to create one tiny moment that signals to your nervous system: *I've done what I can, and I'm ready enough.*
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the idea of it being "tiny" — that actually feels less overwhelming than what I was picturing, like I'd need to find twenty quiet minutes I definitely don't have. But I'm a little skeptical that three breaths in a hallway is going to cut through the kind of spiral I get into before an exam, where my heart is already racing and I'm convinced I blanked on everything I studied. It feels like putting a bandage on something that needs stitches, if that makes sense.
therapist: Your analogy is actually really sharp, and the way you're speaking — soft but quick, like your mind is moving faster than you want it to — tells me you're genuinely engaging with this, not just dismissing it. You're right that three breaths alone won't rewire a deep spiral, and I don't want to oversell it — but the breaths aren't the stitches, *you* are, and what we're building here is the larger wound care: understanding the pattern, challenging the "I've already failed" story, and practicing accessing your own evidence before panic erases it. The breath is just the door you walk through to get to all of that.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I like that — "you are the stitches" — that actually lands differently than I expected it to. But I guess what scares me is that I don't trust myself to be a reliable wound care provider, you know? Like, the whole problem is that when I'm in the spiral, I become the worst possible version of myself to be in charge of anything, let alone my own mind.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, with that high, almost fragile quality in your voice — really reflects what you're saying, like a part of you is genuinely afraid of letting yourself down in that moment. But I want to gently challenge the idea that the "spiral version" of you is your real self in charge — that version is anxiety *overriding* you, not *replacing* you, and the fact that you can describe it this clearly right now means your wiser self is very much present. Building self-trust doesn't start in the exam room under pressure; it starts in moments exactly like this one, where you're learning to recognize the spiral for what it is rather than believing everything it tells you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like that spiral version is exactly who I become when it matters most. Like, right now in this room I can talk about it clearly, but that almost makes it worse somehow, because I know that clarity just disappears the second I sit down in front of that exam paper. It feels like there are two completely different people, and I have no control over which one shows up.
therapist: The way your voice carries that high, strained quality right now tells me this particular fear — of losing yourself when it counts — sits somewhere really deep and painful. What you're describing feels like two separate people, but I'd offer a different frame: it's actually one person, you, with access to different mental states, and the clarity you have *right now* isn't separate from you — it's something you're actively building, like a muscle that gets stronger each time you name the spiral instead of being swallowed by it. The goal of our work together isn't to guarantee which version "shows up," but to make the grounded version of you harder and harder for anxiety to fully silence.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but honestly it feels a little too neat. Like, when I'm in the middle of it — when I'm standing there and my mind just goes blank and I say something I don't mean or I freeze completely — it doesn't feel like a "different mental state," it feels like I've just... disappeared. And I guess what scares me is that if I can't trust myself to show up when it actually matters, how do I trust that this "muscle" you're talking about is even real, and not just something that sounds good in a therapy room?
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, high, and strained — even as your words are measured and questioning, tells me this isn't skepticism for its own sake; this is a real and tender fear that hope itself might be another thing that lets you down. And I want to honor that completely, because "it sounds good in a therapy room" is one of the most honest things a client can say to me — you're right to demand that it be real, not just reassuring. The muscle isn't proven by what I say here; it's proven incrementally, in small moments outside this room, and that's exactly why we work slowly and concretely — not to hand you a neat answer, but to help you gather your own evidence that *you* decide whether to trust.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate that you're not just brushing off what I said, and yeah, you're right that it's not really skepticism — it's more like... I've gotten my hopes up before and it just made the crash worse. Like, the loneliness doesn't go away just because I understand it better, you know? I guess I'm just scared that gathering "evidence" is going to feel like another thing I fail at if it doesn't work out the way it's supposed to.
therapist: The quietness in your voice right now, even as your pitch carries something almost fragile and exposed, tells me this just became about something much bigger than exams — and I want to stay with that, because what you're describing, the fear that hope itself becomes evidence of failure, is one of the loneliest places a person can be. I want to gently reframe what "evidence gathering" means here: it's not a test you pass or fail, it's simply noticing what happens, and even a crash after hope is information, not proof that you're broken. The loneliness you're naming — that understanding something doesn't make it hurt less — that's real, and it deserves more than a technique; it deserves to be heard, and I hear it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
